result.summary: Pindar summons the daughters of Kadmos to Apollo's Ismenian shrine to honour Thebes and Thrasydaios' Pythian victory. He tells of Orestes' rescue and the murder of Agamemnon, then breaks off, reflects on moderation and condemns tyranny, and ends by praising Iolaos, Kastor and Polydeukes.

scenes.title: Editorial note on the date
scenes.summary: A note dates the victory to 478 B.C. and says little else is certain about the Theban allusions.

scenes.title: Summoning the Theban heroines
scenes.summary: Pindar calls Semele, Ino and the other daughters of Kadmos to the Ismenian shrine to sing of Thebes and Thrasydaios' third victory.

scenes.title: Orestes and Agamemnon's murder
scenes.summary: Orestes is saved by his nurse Arsinoë while Klytaimnestra kills Agamemnon and Kassandra. Pindar asks her motive, then recounts Orestes' stay with Strophios and his revenge.
scenes.stakes: Orestes' life as a child; later Agamemnon's life and Orestes' duty of vengeance.

scenes.title: Pindar checks his course
scenes.summary: Pindar says he has wandered from his path and calls on the Muse to return to praise Thrasydaios and his father.

scenes.title: Moderation and heroic glory
scenes.summary: Pindar praises the family's racing victories, favours the middle course and condemns tyranny, and ends with Iolaos, Kastor and Polydeukes.

alias_notes.explanation: A title of Apollo as god of oracles.
The name Ino bore as a sea goddess.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar's political creed: the middle course is best and tyranny is condemned.
Memorable maxim that prosperity attracts envy while obscurity escapes notice.

analysis.text: The ode contrasts Orestes' violent family with the ideal of moderation, warning against excess and envy.
Composed after Plataea, the praise of the middle course and rejection of tyranny reflects Thebes' troubled politics after the Persian Wars.

legacy.text: Pindar's version of Orestes' rescue by his nurse, here called Arsinoë, is an early variant of the myth later dramatized by the Athenian tragedians.

fun_facts.text: Pindar's Pythian 11 is among his shorter odes, and its abrupt break from Orestes is a famous example of his digressive style.

language_notes.text: Semele (mother of Dionysos) and Ino, daughters of Kadmos, became divinities; Ino was changed into the sea-goddess Leukothea. The mother of Herakles is Alkmene.
Loxias is Apollo's title as oracle-giver, 'the Ambiguous one'; Pytho is Delphi, and the 'Earth-navel' is its sacred stone.
'Soul sped to the shadowy shore of Acheron' means Agamemnon and Kassandra were killed and sent to the underworld, Acheron being a river of the dead.
Agamemnon had sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia at Aulis, on the Euripos strait, to gain winds for Troy; Klytaimnestra's anger is traditionally traced to this.
'Habitations of softness' means the luxurious, delicate dwellings of Troy, which Agamemnon burned.
Pindar says he has gone astray at a place where three roads meet, a figure for losing the thread of his poem.
The Muse is said to have promised a loan for 'silver', alluding to Pindar being paid for his odes.
Kastor and Polydeukes, the Dioscuri, spent alternate days among the dead at Therapnai and among the gods on Olympus.

context_notes.text: Plataea (479 B.C.) ended the Persian invasion of Greece; Thebes had sided with Persia and was punished afterwards.
The Ismenion was Apollo's temple at Thebes, where prophecy was given by tripods.
Orestes was Agamemnon's son; he was smuggled away as a child after his father's murder by Klytaimnestra and Aigisthos.
Strophios of Phokis was Pylades' father and sheltered Orestes; Orestes later returned and killed his mother and Aigisthos.
Pindar, an aristocrat, praises the moderate middle station, as safer than the extremes of poverty or great power.

literary_notes.text: Pindar addresses the Theban heroines directly, summoning them as a divine chorus to celebrate the victory.
This general maxim about envy turns the story into a moral observation about fame and obscurity.
Pindar compares his digression to a boat blown off course by the wind, picturing the poem as a voyage.
Excellence borne modestly is set against insolence, and death is called gracious because of the honourable name left behind.
